issues.item: Triggers: Auditory (Explosion): Explosion or bang sounds
issues.explanation: For a mugging/robbery trauma, 'explosion or bang sounds' is a poor fit unless there was a firearm discharge or similar blast-like cue; nothing else in the profile suggests that context, so this trigger is clinically hard to reconcile with the trauma type and the rest of the selected items.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Lost Community: I have lost my connection to my community and culture
issues.explanation: 'I have lost my connection to my community and culture' is difficult to justify from the rest of this profile for an adult European married teacher after a mugging/robbery. The other appraisals focus on self-blame/institutional failure, but this item implies a broader cultural/community rupture that is not supported by the trauma type, demographics, or other nodes.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Violated Values: I acted in ways that go against who I am
issues.explanation: For a mugging/robbery trauma, the profile otherwise centers on external danger, sensory reliving, and mistrust/injustice. 'Violated Values' implies the patient did something morally incongruent during the event, but there are no accompanying memory, threat, trigger, or strategy items suggesting perpetration, betrayal of others, failure to act, or shame-based self-condemnation. In this profile it stands apart from the rest of the formulation and is the least clinically coherent item.

vignette:
Daniel, a 38-year-old European American high school teacher, described the mugging as the moment his ordinary sense of safety split open. It happened on an early winter evening after he left a grocery store near his home, carrying a bag of food and walking to his car in the lot. Two men came up fast from between parked vehicles, one crowding his shoulder while the other barked at him to hand over his wallet. Daniel remembered the metallic taste in his mouth when one of them shoved him against the car and he caught the smell of cold pavement, exhaust, and his own fear. In the weeks that followed, the memory would not stay in the past; when it broke through, it arrived with such force that it felt completely real across all his senses at once, and he could taste that same metallic edge as if he were back in the lot. He said it often forced its way into his mind when he did not want it to, especially when something around him resembled the scene enough to open the door.

Crowded places became the clearest and most painful reminder. The packed supermarket aisle, the school hallway between classes, and especially the crush of parents at basketball games could pull him straight back into that evening, and once the memory surfaced, it seemed to bring the whole event with it. Each time Daniel found himself in those crowded spaces, the thought arrived with it that this was what life had become for him now: a man who would never feel relaxed in a room full of people, always braced for the next shove or confrontation. Daniel found that after a vivid surge of reliving, he became convinced that the world was a dangerous place and that what had happened to him was deeply unfair, made worse by the belief that the people or institutions that should have protected him let him down. He felt angry that nothing had been done about it in any meaningful way, and that sense of injustice fed the memory itself; the more he dwelt on how wrong it was, the more the event seemed to reassert itself with the same taste, the same fear, the same helplessness. When he told himself he should have been more alert, or that he had been left on his own when someone should have helped, those thoughts seemed to pull him right back into the parking lot, making the memory sharper and harder to shake. Even driving with other people could set this off, because being trapped in a car with someone else nearby reminded him of how vulnerable he had felt pinned in the lot, and from there the same thoughts about danger and abandonment returned.

Once the memory had taken hold, Daniel became intensely watchful. He studied people's faces and body language to detect if they were a threat, scanning the expressions of strangers in the grocery store checkout line and the posture of men walking too close on the sidewalk. He scanned exits as soon as he entered any room or building, as if every classroom, restaurant, or church hall needed a quick map in case he had to get out. Unexpected movement nearby caused him to react as if he were in danger; a student reaching suddenly across a desk, a person turning quickly in a crowded corridor, even a car door slamming in the parking lot could make him jerk and brace himself. That constant vigilance seemed to confirm his worst assumptions. Because he was always checking for signs of threat, he found more moments that looked unsafe, and each one strengthened his belief that the world was dangerous and that no one could be counted on to keep him safe. Feeling that constant danger everywhere he went became, for Daniel, the clearest proof that his life had changed for good; the fear itself seemed to tell him that he was not the kind of person who could move through the world safely anymore. The fear also pushed his attention back toward the memory, which returned more readily when he was already keyed up. And once that memory had come back so vividly, ordinary things around him started to feel like warnings: a cart rattling too close in the grocery store, a student's sudden movement across a desk, or a car door shutting hard in the lot could all take on the same charged quality as that night.

As his threat monitoring narrowed his life, the triggers multiplied. The crowded places he once moved through without thought now felt loaded with potential danger, and the first sign of bodies pressing too close would send him back into the memory and the anger attached to it. Living at that pitch of alertness, he began reading reminders into almost everything - a cluster of people at the school entrance, a van idling too long outside the supermarket, a sudden burst of voices in a hallway - each one confirming what his body had already decided was true. Loud noises carried similar force. The bang of a dropped binder in his classroom, a truck backfiring near the school entrance, or a sudden shout in a crowded corridor could make him jump hard enough that students noticed. After each startle, he was left more convinced that he had to keep scanning, which made him even more alert to faces, exits, and movement. Daniel had begun taking longer routes through the building to avoid hallways at passing time, and he chose to drive alone whenever he could; when he had to carpool with a colleague for an evening event, he sat rigidly, watching mirrors and shoulders instead of talking. Over months, those habits narrowed his teaching life and made him quieter at home, where his wife noticed that he seemed to arrive carrying an invisible tension.

By the time he sought help, Daniel felt worn down by the loop between what he remembered, what he feared, and what he could no longer ignore. He came in because he was exhausted by the constant sense that danger was lurking in ordinary places, and because he did not want his world to keep shrinking around crowded rooms, loud sounds, and every sudden movement. What frightened him most was the suspicion that if he stopped scanning, he would be caught off guard again; what he hoped for, though he could barely say it without feeling foolish, was to walk into a room, hear a noise, or sit in a car with other people without instantly feeling that same old mugging closing in on him.

violations.explanation: The vignette shows triggers leading to re-experiencing the memory, but it does not clearly state that triggers drive Daniel’s negative appraisals or beliefs.
It describes negative beliefs after reliving, but does not show those appraisals causing the memory to return.
It shows triggers bring back the memory, but not that the memory itself creates or generates new triggers.
The vignette shows threat monitoring reinforcing danger beliefs, but not that perceived threat directly leads to negative appraisals in the same paragraph.
It shows threat monitoring and scanning for danger, but not that threat directly produces specific triggers or reminders.

vignette_attempts.feedback:
REQUIRED EDGES MISSING:
- Triggers → Negative Appraisals: The vignette shows triggers leading to re-experiencing the memory, but it does not clearly state that triggers drive Daniel’s negative appraisals or beliefs.
  e.g. "Every time she walked through that car park, the thought arrived with her: this is what your life is now — flinching at nothing."
  e.g. "Seeing a man in the same jacket made her think, with quiet certainty, that she would never stop being afraid."
  e.g. "The sound of raised voices next door told her, with a logic she couldn't argue with, that nowhere was ever really safe."
- Negative Appraisals → Memory: It describes negative beliefs after reliving, but does not show those appraisals causing the memory to return.
  e.g. "The belief that she was permanently changed kept bringing her back to the moment it had happened, as if she needed to locate exactly where she had been lost."
  e.g. "Telling herself that she should have seen it coming made the memory more vivid and easier to find — it sat there waiting, proof of her failure."
  e.g. "The conviction that she was weak fed directly into the flashback, colouring it, making it worse: she wasn't just there again, she was there again and helpless."
- Memory → Triggers: It shows triggers bring back the memory, but not that the memory itself creates or generates new triggers.
  e.g. "After the memory had surfaced, even the most ordinary things — a kettle whistling, a door slamming — felt like warnings she couldn't afford to ignore."
  e.g. "The intrusive image left her scanning every room she entered, cataloguing exits, tracking faces, unable to switch off."
  e.g. "Because the memory came back so vividly, she began to see threads of it everywhere: in strangers' faces, in certain times of day, in the quality of winter light."
- Threat → Negative Appraisals: The vignette shows threat monitoring reinforcing danger beliefs, but not that perceived threat directly leads to negative appraisals in the same paragraph.
  e.g. "The constant sense of danger was the most convincing proof she had that her life had changed beyond repair."
  e.g. "Feeling this afraid all the time, she had eventually come to accept the conclusion her body kept offering: that she was not the kind of person who got to feel safe."
  e.g. "The threat that shadowed her days quietly confirmed the thought she worked hardest to resist — that this was simply who she was now."
- Threat → Triggers: It shows threat monitoring and scanning for danger, but not that threat directly produces specific triggers or reminders.
  e.g. "Already running on threat, she found that almost anything could tip into a warning — a van parked at an odd angle, a light left on that shouldn't have been."
  e.g. "The background hum of danger she carried everywhere made ordinary cues feel like messages — each one confirming what her body already believed."
  e.g. "Living at that pitch of alertness, she found the world had become dense with reminders she couldn't stop reading."
